newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Taleban seize key airbase north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban seize key airbase north of Kabul.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia captured the key Bagram military airbase north of Kabul on Thursday, a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted witnesses as saying the Taleban had gained control of the base after a fierce battle in the morning, in which at least 12 opposition fighters and three Taleban militiamen were killed.
They said seven Taleban fighters had been wounded in the two-pronged assault from the Qarabagh area to the south and the village of Bagram to the west of the battered airfield.

The Soviet-built base, about 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, fell to the purist Taleban after they captured Kabul on September 27, but was retaken by former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood on October 18.

The Taleban grabbed it back on December 27, but could only hold it for a few hours. If they can keep it this time, it would mark a significant psychological reversal for Masood and his powerful ally, northern Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
When opposition forces captured it in October, there were eight apparently useless fighter jets, several transport aircraft and helicopter carcasses parked on the tarmac.
The base, sitting on a dusty plain with snowcapped peaks in the background, was used by Soviet forces in the 1980s to support a communist-backed government in Kabul.
The latest fighting came a day after peace talks between the Taleban and its opponents ended inconclusively in Islamabad.
The United Nations Special Mission to Afghanistan (UNSMA), headed by Norbert Holl, had organised the three-day meeting that grouped three representatives from each side.

UNSMA said the talks had achieved agreement on several key points. "These included the urgency of an immediate ceasefire in Afghanistan and the need to view this ceasefire as a first and major step toward a lasting political process and dialogue rather than as an end in itself," it said on Wednesday.
It said that the participants had no decision-making powers but had agreed to return for more talks next month.
However, Maulvi Shahabuddin Dilawar, counsellor at the Taleban-controlled Afghan consulate in Peshawar, told AIP the attack on Bagram had been launched because the talks had failed.
"The Taleban held talks to show the people they also believe in talks, but regretted that there was no outcome," he said.

UNSMA said the talks had focused on implementation of a ceasefire, formation of a commission to supervise and monitor it, demilitarisation of Kabul, exchange of prisoners, and "creation of suitable conditions for the establishment of a broad-based and fully representative government".
The Taleban, which control about two-thirds of Afghanistan, are battling opposition forces in remote northwestern provinces as well as on the shifting frontlines north of Kabul.
